title: Brewing another binary in the Teapot: Nandou=Phi Sagittarii
summary: The iconic Teapot asterism in Sagittarius is particularly rich in intermediate-mass stars in multiple systems. Here we combine VLTI/GRAVITY, archival spectroscopic observations, past radial velocity measurements and photometry to solve for the orbital and stellar parameters of the binary Nandou=Phi Sagittarii. It has a period $P=238.844\pm0.011$ days, a semi-major axis $a=1.32\pm0.10\text{ au}$ and eccentricity $e=0.418\pm0.004$. The precision in the dynamical masses $M_A=3.8\pm0.9 M_{\odot}$ and $M_B=1.6\pm0.4 M_{\odot}$ is currently limited by the parallax $p=12.5\pm1.0 \text{ mas}$. We find that the original Hipparcos 1997 Intermediate Astrometric Data (IAD) are consistent with the expected photocenter semi-major axis $a_{\mathrm{phot}} \sim 5 \text{ mas}$, while the IAD from the Hipparcos 2007 new reduction yield a too small $a_{\mathrm{phot}} = 1.7\pm0.3 \text{ mas}$, confirming the suspicion that a too aggressive modeling of the satellite attitude can lead to overfitting that suppresses the orbital motion. Matching the primary's temperature $T_{\mathrm{eff,A}} = 12000\pm250 \text{ K}$ and radius $R_{\mathrm{A}} = 5.1\pm 0.4 R_{\odot}$ to stellar evolutionary models implies that it is a $M_A \simeq 4 M_{\odot}$ star near the end of the main-sequence. Nandou will eventually most likely become a symbiotic star.

title: The spatial structure of solar magnetoconvection at scales up to $60$~Mm
summary: While convective motions at the scale of granules on the solar surface are well understood, those of mesogranular and supergranulation are not. At still larger scales, the lack of giant cells is a major mystery. We aim to slightly improve understanding of the radial and horizontal flows associated at mesogranular scales and supergranulation. We perform a deep MURaM small-scale dynamo simulation, extending from $50$~Mm below the solar surface and with a horizontal size of 60~Mm and sufficient resolution to begin to properly resolve the magnetic bright points in intergranular lanes. We determine the structure of the convective modes from the simulations at different scales, and compare the power spectra to those which have been previously observed. At all scales which are resolved by the simulation the simulated flows agree with the amplitude implied by Doppler measurements and local correlation tracking (LCT) measurements. The power in the vertical Doppler velocities at supergranular and larger scales is shown to be influenced by density perturbations near the surface. The structure of the modes at depth is simple as expected from the previous study of \cite{LordCameron2014} except the horizontal forcing scale scales like $H_ρ^{2/3}$ instead of $Hρ$. The simulations reproduce the observations up to scales of $60$~Mm. Within the simulated range, $l>=70$, we do not see the excess power associated with the convective conundrum.

title: How fast is the fastest-rotating O-type star in the Galaxy?
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure and 2 tables, A&A Accepted
summary: {Rapid rotation distorts massive stars, making parameters from spherical models inclination-dependent. We studied these effects in the extreme Galactic O-type runaway LAMOST J040643.69+542347.8.} {We re-determined its stellar and rotational parameters with an oblate, gravity-darkened photospheric model and tabulated Stark profiles for selected \ion{He}{ii} lines.} {We fitted continuum-normalised spectra over 4000--4600\,Å with \texttt{ZPEKTR}, using TLUSTY/SYNSPEC emergent fluxes, limb darkening to weight their angular contribution over the visible Roche surface, Espinosa-Lara \& Rieutord gravity darkening, and Schöning--Butler Stark profiles. Interstellar and wind- or circumstellar-dominated features were masked.} {The model reproduces \ion{He}{ii}~$\lambda4200$, \ion{He}{i}~$\lambda4471$, and \ion{He}{ii}~$\lambda4542$. We obtained parent non-rotating counterpart (PNRC) parameters $T_{\rm eff}^{\rm PNRC}=38\,716\pm1041$~K, $\log g^{\rm PNRC}=4.12\pm0.12$, and $v_{\rm e}\sin i=587\pm73$~\kps. The central grid solution gives $Ω/Ω_{\rm c}=0.93$, $v_{\rm e}/v_{\rm c}=0.77$, $i=65^\circ$, $R_{\rm e}/R_{\rm p}=1.25$, and an equatorial centrifugal-to-gravitational acceleration ratio $η_{\rm e}=0.50$. Roche critical rotation requires $η_{\rm e}=1$ and $R_{\rm e}/R_{\rm p}=1.5$: despite the high angular rate, the central solution is not critical in equatorial force balance. The projected velocity exceeds, but is statistically consistent with, the previous spherical-fit value.} {\object{LAMOST J040643.69+542347.8} has a markedly oblate, gravity-darkened photosphere. Its proximity to critical rotation should be assessed using $Ω/Ω_{\rm c}$, $v_{\rm e}/v_{\rm c}$, and $η_{\rm e}$ together. A controlled spherical fit with the same atmosphere grid is needed to isolate the bias from neglecting deformation and gravity darkening.}

title: Photometric Study of a Distant SU UMa-type Dwarf Nova KSP-OT-201803a
summary: We present the discovery and photometric study of a distant dwarf nova KSP-OT-201803a using BVI-band observation data obtained by using the KMTNet Supernova Program. One superoutburst (SO) and three normal outbursts are identified from two years of observations (2018-2019), which show that KSP-OT-201803a is an SU UMa-type dwarf nova (DN). Applying the phase dispersion minimization method to the superhump data during the plateau phase of the SO yields a superhump period of P_sh = 127.4 minutes (=2.123 hr =0.08847 days). By stacking ten images of the quiescent phase, we find the quiescent phase magnitude of V = 22.59 +/- 0.18 mag. The SO shows quiescent-to-peak amplitude of 4.97 +/- 0.18 mag and duration of 16.59 days which are typical for the SU UMa-type DNe. Using the superhump period-orbital period relation of SU UMa stars, we obtain the approximate distance of 3.7 +/- 0.3 kpc to KSP-OT-201803a and Galactocentric distance of 9.4 kpc and height from the Galactic plane of +1.2 kpc. Stars at these large distances may belong to the Galactic halo or thick disk, which contain old, metal-poor Population II stars; therefore, these systems may have undergone a different evolutionary process than Population I objects. The orbital period gap of DNe spans 2.45-3.18 hours. Assuming that the orbital period of KSP-OT-201803a is a few percent shorter than its superhump period, KSP-OT-201803a may have just emerged from the period gap and recently resumed mass transfer after crossing its lower boundary.

title: Frequent Optical Flares in an M-type Detached Eclipsing Binary TIC 349005337
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 9 tables; accepted by ApJ
summary: A comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic analysis of TIC 349005337, a highly active M-type detached eclipsing binary with an orbital period of 2.6079133 days, is presented utilizing high-cadence and long-term monitoring photometry from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and medium-resolution spectroscopy from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST). By integrating radial velocity curves with light curves, we determined the fundamental physical parameters for both components. The system consists of an M-dwarf primary ($M_1 = 0.517 \pm 0.009 M_\odot$, $R_1 = 0.518 \pm 0.003 R_\odot$) and a fully convective secondary ($M_2 = 0.298 \pm 0.004 M_\odot$, $R_2 = 0.357 \pm 0.003 R_\odot$). A total of 12 high-energy stellar flares, with the most energetic event reaching $3.87 \times 10^{34}$ erg, is identified, confirming the system is in a state of magnetic hyper-activity. The frequent superflares suggest that intense magnetic activity and significant starspot coverage play a dominant role in altering the stellar atmospheric structure. As the secondary component falls below the fully convective boundary, these energetic flares provide critical empirical constraints for distributed dynamo models in the low-mass regime. Our results highlight TIC 349005337 as an ideal laboratory for investigating the interplay between binary dynamics, magnetic reconnection, and the resulting impact on the atmospheric stability of potential orbiting exoplanets.

title: Collective Characterization of Polar Crown Filament Eruptions
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Polar crown filaments (PCFs) are crucially related to the structure of solar polar magnetic fields. They are physically significant because of the ``rush-to-the-pole'' motion, which is an indicator of the poleward drift of magnetic fields from decayed active regions. The formation and evolution of PCFs offer important insights into the Sun's magnetic activity at high latitudes and the solar cycle variation. In this study, we present a collective analysis of 50 PCF disappearance events covering solar cycle 24 and 25. Among them, 24 show rotational motions, and nine have sufficiently clear magnetic configurations for comparison with numerical model predictions. In all nine events, the observed rotation directions agree with the model predictions, suggesting possible magnetic-flux-rope-like structures in these events. All except one of the PCFs in our sample disappeared through eruption rather than thermal disappearance, and most associated CMEs were slow ($<800$ km s$^{-1}$). For events accompanied by transient coronal holes, the estimated magnetic flux associated with the dimming regions is on the order of $10^{20}$--$10^{21}$ Mx. Time--distance analysis identifies 22 events with a clear slow-rise to fast-rise transition, with onset heights ranging from several tens to about 160 Mm and a mean onset velocity of about 2.8 km s$^{-1}$ after excluding the highest-velocity event. Together, these findings characterize the magnetic structure and dynamics of PCF eruptions.

title: Tiny Quiet-Sun EUV Ejections Revealed by High-resolution Multiwavelength Observations
summary: We investigate two successive tiny quiet-Sun EUV ejections on 2022 October 29 using coordinated Solar Orbiter/EUI, IRIS, SDO/AIA, and Goode Solar Telescope observations. We examine their low-lying geometry and the chromospheric and transition-region response before and between the releases. A curved H-alpha thread is present beforehand, and Mg ii and Si iv spectra reveal a compact multithermal precursor 2.6--2.7 min before the first EUV brightening. EUI--AIA stereoscopy places the recurrent compact EUV kernel near 2.2 Mm and the sampled emission at approximately 0.6--4.2 Mm along inclined, locally arched structures. The first ejection shows multithreaded, helical-looking EUV strands; the second shows straighter strands and a decrease in the cross-ridge separation of redshifted and blueshifted Mg ii k3 samples from 1.47'' to 0.89''. Nevertheless, the two peaks have comparable emission-measure increments and estimated event-associated thermal contents of a few 10^26 erg under the same assumptions. Before the second ejection, the regional Si iv and k3 blueshift signals remain enhanced, while the Mg ii central reversal along the activated ridge remains shallower than before the event. Component reconnection between the curved structure and the surrounding field offers a possible explanation. The observations show that jet-like EUV emission can occur in low-lying structures. The second ejection begins before the chromospheric and transition-region spectra have returned to their pre-event states. Its spectral signatures may therefore depend on the atmospheric changes associated with the first ejection as well as on the additional energy input.

title: Spectroscopic diagnostics of coronal fan loops using EIS/Hinode and AIA/SDO
summary: We utilize spectroscopic and imaging data from the EIS/Hinode and the AIA/SDO to determine plasma and wave parameters along coronal fan loops. We determined the temperature along the loop lengths using the EM-loci method with EIS spectral lines and identified multi-thermal plasma components at temperatures ranging from 0.8-1.05, 1.2-1.4, and 1.6-1.8 MK. We further compared these temperature distributions along the loops with those derived from DEM analysis carried out using AIA coronal passbands. The multi-thermal nature of coronal fan loops can be well resolved using EIS spectroscopic data. We determined the density along the loop using the line-ratio method from the EIS Fe XII line pair. We found that density decreases slowly from the expected hydrostatic equilibrium. Our results demonstrate the multi-thermal nature of overdense loops, which can be well resolved with EIS spectroscopic data. We also determined the velocity amplitude of Alfvén waves from the non-thermal broadening of EIS Fe XII spectral line profiles. We further estimated the Alfvén wave energy flux in the corona by combining these parameters with the recently reported magnetic field strength of $\approx$200 G at the coronal footpoint of fan loops. The estimated Alfvén wave energy flux is $\approx$ 2$\times 10^7$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, significantly higher than those reported in earlier studies, and can contribute to coronal losses due to radiation along the fan loops in the active region.

title: Magnetism among the oldest white dwarfs in the solar neighbourhood
summary: We present a new circular polarisation survey of approximately 100 white dwarfs selected as featureless DC stars and combine our measurements with previous observations. Our compilation contains 205 objects, of which 24 show firm circular polarisation detections, while another four show marginal signals that require confirmation. Four magnetic white dwarfs originally classified as DC show polarisation spectra with significant contributions from spectral lines. Depending on the treatment of these objects and of the marginal detections, the inferred fraction of magnetic objects in the DC selected sample lies between approximately 10 and 14%. Among objects without identifiable line contributions, the circular polarisation never exceeds approximately 2%, substantially below the levels observed in some hotter magnetic white dwarfs with prominent spectral features. This is unlikely a symptom of field decay, since in our sample we find no significant evidence for a dependence of magnetic incidence on cooling age, and magnetic fields are detected in stars with cooling ages exceeding 9 Gyr. Instead, strong spectral line opacity provides a natural mechanism for producing much larger polarisation amplitudes than the continuum. In the full sample considered here, the incidence of detectable magnetism increases with stellar mass. Most average-mass magnetic stars for which repeated observations are available show no clear polarimetric variability, whereas variability appears more common among the most massive objects.

title: Population synthesis of substellar companions surviving common-envelope evolution
summary: Predicting the population of substellar companions around white dwarfs (WDs) requires accounting for both companions that avoid engulfment during stellar evolution and those that survive common-envelope (CE) evolution. While the former population was investigated in our previous population-synthesis study, a comprehensive population synthesis of the latter remains lacking. We investigated the fate of engulfed substellar companions within the same population-synthesis framework. We aim to predict the occurrence rates and properties of companions surviving CE evolution, identify the conditions permitting survival, and assess their detectability. We determined the stellar structure at the onset of CE evolution and calculated CE outcomes for different ejection efficiencies considering gravitational and thermal energy or the full internal energy of the envelope. Survival is rare and strongly depends on the evolutionary stage at engulfment. No companions entering CE evolution during the red-giant branch or early asymptotic-giant branch survive. Survivors originate exclusively from the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant branch, when stellar envelopes can become weakly bound, allowing even relatively low-mass companions to survive. The resulting systems typically have orbital periods of a few hours. We predict occurrence rates of up to 0.16% among WDs, corresponding to an upper limit of 2.53 companions to WDs within 50 pc. Transit detection is primarily limited by orbital geometry, whereas all predicted survivors would produce detectable infrared excess with JWST out to 50pc. We predict that CE evolution produces a small but observable population of close substellar companions to WDs. Survival is governed not only by companion mass but critically by the envelope structure at engulfment, particularly during thermal pulses, and by the contribution of recombination energy to envelope ejection.

title: The formation and evolution of Wolf-Rayet stars with temperature-dependent winds
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: Massive stars strongly influence their environments through their radiation, stellar winds and core-collapse supernovae, while their own evolution is strongly shaped by wind mass loss. Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are characterised by strong, optically thick winds, and the implementation of these winds remains an important uncertainty in stellar evolution models. Recent hydrodynamically consistent atmosphere calculations predict WR mass-loss rates that depend strongly on the temperature at the wind-launching region. We investigate the effects of incorporating these latest theoretical WR wind prescriptions into single and binary stellar evolution models at Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) metallicities. We find that the temperature dependence of the WR wind can significantly alter the evolution of stars near the threshold for WR formation. In particular, an implementation that transitions from a hydrogen rich WNL wind prescription to a classical WR wind driven by the hot iron opacity bump causes some SMC-metallicity models to spend an extended period at temperatures of approximately 70 to 90 kK. This produces a concentration of models in the temperature range occupied by most observed SMC WR stars, a feature that has previously been difficult to explain with stellar evolution models. Our results demonstrate that incorporating physically motivated, temperature dependent WR winds can improve the agreement between stellar evolution models and observed WR populations.
